headline: Is a Whole House Surge Protector Worth It in Sioux Falls?
description: Is a whole house surge protector worth it in Sioux Falls? What it covers, what it can't stop, when SD code requires one, and when to call (605) 250-4838.
about: Whole house surge protectors for Sioux Falls, South Dakota homes
keywords: is a whole house surge protector worth it, Sioux Falls, whole house surge protector, surge protective device, panel surge protection, South Dakota electrical code

mainEntity.name: Is a whole house surge protector worth it if I already use power strips?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually, yes. Strips only guard what is plugged into them. The furnace, air conditioner, range, washer, dryer and garage door opener are wired or plugged in where a strip can't help. Keep your strips on TVs and computers and add the panel device for the rest.

mainEntity.name: Will a whole house surge protector stop lightning damage?

acceptedAnswer.text: No device can promise that. A direct strike can still damage equipment. A panel surge protector is built for surges that come in on the power lines, such as a nearby strike or a utility switching event, plus the smaller surges made inside your home.

mainEntity.name: Is a whole house surge protector required in South Dakota?

acceptedAnswer.text: For new or replaced services, yes. South Dakota inspects permits under the 2023 National Electrical Code, which requires a surge protective device on services supplying homes. A house with an older panel that isn't being changed generally isn't forced to add one.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my surge protector still works?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most panel devices have an indicator light. Check it after big storms and a few times a year. If the light shows a fault or is out, the device may have used itself up and should be checked and replaced. Don't open the panel yourself.

mainEntity.name: Can a surge protector be added to my existing panel?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often, yes. It usually needs an open breaker space or a side mount, plus a working ground path. A full, damaged or outdated panel may need repair or an upgrade first. An electrician checks this before anything is installed.
